old:
In large firms the owners (shareholders) do not run the business — managers do. This separation of ownership and control means managers may pursue their own objectives — higher salaries, sales maximisation, perks — instead of the owners' goal of profit maximisation.

Solutions align incentives: performance-related pay, bonuses and stock options that make managers gain when shareholders do.

old:
Public sector — owned and funded by the government, usually to provide services in the public interest (the NHS). Private sector — owned by individuals or shareholders, usually profit-motivated.

Profit organisations aim to generate financial returns for owners; not-for-profit organisations, such as charities, reinvest any surplus in their social purpose instead.
new:
• Public sector — owned and funded by the government, usually to provide services in the public interest (the NHS).
  • Private sector — owned by individuals or shareholders, usually profit-motivated.

Profit organisations aim to generate financial returns for owners.

Not-for-profit organisations, such as charities, reinvest any surplus in their social purpose instead.

old:
Horizontal — merging with a competitor at the same stage of production (two car manufacturers), raising market share. Vertical — merging along the supply chain: backward with a supplier (a car maker buying a tyre maker) to secure inputs; forward with a distributor to secure outlets and margin.

Conglomerate — merging with an unrelated business, spreading risk across markets.
new:
• Horizontal — merging with a competitor at the same stage of production (two car manufacturers), raising market share.
  • Vertical — merging along the supply chain: backward with a supplier (a car maker buying a tyre maker) to secure inputs; forward with a distributor to secure outlets and margin.
  • Conglomerate — merging with an unrelated business, spreading risk across markets.

old:
Market size — niche or saturated markets cap expansion, pushing firms to internationalise. Access to finance — smaller firms look riskier, so borrowing is harder and dearer. Owner objectives — lifestyle goals or satisficing over rapid growth.

Regulation — competition policy (the CMA) can block mergers that create too much market power, and rules on demerit goods can cap whole markets.
new:
• Market size — niche or saturated markets cap expansion, pushing firms to internationalise.
  • Access to finance — smaller firms look riskier, so borrowing is harder and dearer.
  • Owner objectives — lifestyle goals or satisficing over rapid growth.
  • Regulation — competition policy (the CMA) can block mergers that create too much market power, and rules on demerit goods can cap whole markets.

old:
A demerger is when a large firm splits into two or more separate, independent businesses — the opposite of a merger.

Reasons: reduce diseconomies of scale; increase focus on the core business; resolve culture clashes from an earlier merger; shed loss-making divisions; raise capital; or regulatory pressure — the CMA can force a demerger to cut monopoly power.
new:
A demerger is when a large firm splits into two or more separate, independent businesses — the opposite of a merger.

Reasons:

  • Reduce diseconomies of scale.
  • Increase focus on the core business.
  • Resolve culture clashes from an earlier merger.
  • Shed loss-making divisions.
  • Raise capital.
  • Regulatory pressure — the CMA can force a demerger to cut monopoly power.

old:
Business — lower average costs and sharper focus, against transition costs and lost synergies. Workers — better conditions and career paths in focused firms, against redundancies and transition uncertainty.

Consumers — more competition can mean lower prices and better service; but smaller firms may lose scale economies, which can push costs and prices the other way.
new:
• Business — lower average costs and sharper focus, against transition costs and lost synergies.
  • Workers — better conditions and career paths in focused firms, against redundancies and transition uncertainty.
  • Consumers — more competition can mean lower prices and better service; but smaller firms may lose scale economies, which can push costs and prices the other way.

old: Name the four business objectives in the Edexcel specification, with their rules.
new: Name the four business objectives, with their rules.

old:
Profit maximisation — the traditional assumption, maximising shareholder returns: produce where MC = MR. Revenue maximisation — for market share or scale economies: MR = 0. Sales maximisation — grow volume while breaking even: AC = AR.

Satisficing — a satisfactory rather than maximum profit, balancing shareholders against managers' own objectives (the principal-agent problem); output and price lie between the profit-max and sales-max positions.
new:
• Profit maximisation — the traditional assumption, maximising shareholder returns: produce where MC = MR.
  • Revenue maximisation — for market share or scale economies: MR = 0.
  • Sales maximisation — grow volume while breaking even: AC = AR.
  • Satisficing — a satisfactory rather than maximum profit, balancing shareholders against managers' own objectives (the principal-agent problem); output and price lie between the profit-max and sales-max positions.

old: TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings from sales. AR = TR ÷ Q — which simplifies to the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve. MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the additional revenue from selling one more unit.
new:
• TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings from sales.
  • AR = TR ÷ Q — which simplifies to the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve.
  • MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the additional revenue from selling one more unit.

old: Define the seven cost measures in the specification.
new: Define the seven cost measures.

old:
Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries); variable costs vary directly with it (raw materials, hourly wages). TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output: AC = TC ÷ Q, AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q. MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the additional cost of producing one more unit.
new:
• Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries).
  • Variable costs vary directly with it (raw materials, hourly wages).
  • TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output:

  • AC = TC ÷ Q.
  • AFC = TFC ÷ Q.
  • AVC = TVC ÷ Q.

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the additional cost of producing one more unit.

old:
TC = 200 + TVC: 280, 340, 450, 600

AC = TC ÷ Q: 280 ÷ 10 = £28; 340 ÷ 20 = £17; 450 ÷ 30 = £15; 600 ÷ 40 = £15

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ: (340 − 280) ÷ 10 = £6; then £11; then £15

Note where AC stops falling: between 30 and 40 units MC equals AC at £15 — average cost bottoms out exactly where marginal cost catches it.
new:
TC = 200 + TVC: 280, 340, 450, 600

AC = TC ÷ Q:

  • 280 ÷ 10 = £28
  • 340 ÷ 20 = £17
  • 450 ÷ 30 = £15
  • 600 ÷ 40 = £15

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ:

  • (340 − 280) ÷ 10 = £6
  • then £11
  • then £15

Note where AC stops falling: between 30 and 40 units MC equals AC at £15 — average cost bottoms out exactly where marginal cost catches it.

old:
Purchasing — bulk-buying discounts; technical — large-scale machinery affordable only at volume; managerial — specialist managers; financial — cheaper borrowing as lenders see less risk; marketing — advertising spread over more units; risk-bearing — diversification across products and markets.

All are reasons within the business why average costs fall as output grows — they drive the LRAC's falling section.
new:
• Purchasing — bulk-buying discounts.
  • Technical — large-scale machinery affordable only at volume.
  • Managerial — specialist managers.
  • Financial — cheaper borrowing as lenders see less risk.
  • Marketing — advertising spread over more units.
  • Risk-bearing — diversification across products and markets.

All are reasons within the business why average costs fall as output grows — they drive the LRAC's falling section.

old:
Size itself becomes the cost driver: communication stretches across more layers and sites; coordination and control weaken as management grows remote from operations; motivation falls when workers feel like small parts of a vast machine; and bureaucracy multiplies.

This is why growth is not automatically profitable — and why some firms demerge to get back below the point where average costs turn upward.
new:
Size itself becomes the cost driver:

  • Communication stretches across more layers and sites.
  • Coordination and control weaken as management grows remote from operations.
  • Motivation falls when workers feel like small parts of a vast machine.
  • Bureaucracy multiplies.

This is why growth is not automatically profitable — and why some firms demerge to get back below the point where average costs turn upward.

old:
The horizontal price line is tangent to the minimum of AC, and MC passes through the same point: P = MC gives allocative efficiency and minimum AC gives productive efficiency, both at the same output Q.

But with only normal profit there is nothing to reinvest, so dynamic efficiency is unlikely.
new:
The horizontal price line is tangent to the minimum of AC, and MC passes through the same point:

  • P = MC gives allocative efficiency.
  • Minimum AC gives productive efficiency.

Both sit at the same output Q.

But with only normal profit there is nothing to reinvest, so dynamic efficiency is unlikely.

old:
Profit-maximising at MC = MR, the firm stops short of both efficient points: P > MC, so there is allocative inefficiency — underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss — and output lies left of minimum AC, so there is productive inefficiency.

But P > AC means supernormal profit that can be reinvested in R&D — the potential for dynamic efficiency.
new:
Profit-maximising at MC = MR, the firm stops short of both efficient points:

  • P > MC, so there is allocative inefficiency — underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss.
  • Output lies left of minimum AC, so there is productive inefficiency.

But P > AC means supernormal profit that can be reinvested in R&D — the potential for dynamic efficiency.

old:
Prices can go either way: differentiation, branding and weak economies of scale push them up; many firms and easy entry push them down. Quality likewise: competition forces firms to differentiate and improve, but normal-profit margins leave little to invest.

Choice is the clearest gain — many differentiated products — though differentiation can be surface-level, so the variety is not always meaningful.
new:
• Prices can go either way: differentiation, branding and weak economies of scale push them up; many firms and easy entry push them down.
  • Quality likewise: competition forces firms to differentiate and improve, but normal-profit margins leave little to invest.
  • Choice is the clearest gain — many differentiated products — though differentiation can be surface-level, so the variety is not always meaningful.

old:
Collusion is firms agreeing — formally or informally — to restrict supply and raise price, acting like a monopoly to earn supernormal profit. Overt collusion is a formal agreement (a cartel): illegal and provable in court, as when British Airways and Virgin Atlantic fixed fuel surcharges in 2007.

Tacit collusion is an informal understanding, often via price leadership — the market leader sets a price and rivals follow. Same outcome, far harder to prove.
new:
Collusion is firms agreeing — formally or informally — to restrict supply and raise price, acting like a monopoly to earn supernormal profit.

Overt collusion is a formal agreement (a cartel): illegal and provable in court, as when British Airways and Virgin Atlantic fixed fuel surcharges in 2007.

Tacit collusion is an informal understanding, often via price leadership — the market leader sets a price and rivals follow. Same outcome, far harder to prove.

old:
Above the current price demand is elastic: rivals ignore a price rise, so customers switch away and revenue falls. Below it demand is inelastic: rivals match a cut, so few customers arrive and revenue still falls — at worst a price war starts.

The kink makes MR discontinuous at Q, and MC can shift anywhere within the gap without changing the profit-maximising price — so prices stay "sticky" and firms compete through differentiation and advertising instead.
new:
• Above the current price demand is elastic: rivals ignore a price rise, so customers switch away and revenue falls.
  • Below it demand is inelastic: rivals match a cut, so few customers arrive and revenue still falls — at worst a price war starts.

The kink makes MR discontinuous at Q, and MC can shift anywhere within the gap without changing the profit-maximising price — so prices stay "sticky" and firms compete through differentiation and advertising instead.

old:
Price wars — repeated rounds of undercutting that damage every firm's profits. Predatory pricing — temporarily pricing below average cost to drive smaller rivals out and raise prices later; illegal in the UK and US. Limit pricing — pricing low enough that large supernormal profits are unattainable, deterring entry.

Because price competition is so costly, oligopolists usually prefer non-price competition: differentiation, advertising, customer service, convenience and loyalty schemes.
new:
• Price wars — repeated rounds of undercutting that damage every firm's profits.
  • Predatory pricing — temporarily pricing below average cost to drive smaller rivals out and raise prices later; illegal in the UK and US.
  • Limit pricing — pricing low enough that large supernormal profits are unattainable, deterring entry.

Because price competition is so costly, oligopolists usually prefer non-price competition: differentiation, advertising, customer service, convenience and loyalty schemes.
